meta.title: Who really said "Laughter is timeless, imagination has no age, and dreams are forever"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Walt Disney never said "Laughter is timeless, imagination has no age, and dreams are forever." Wikiquote files it as misattributed; the true author is unknown.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'Laughter is timeless, imagination has no age, and dreams are forever'?
meta.ogDescription: Wikiquote lists this line as misattributed to Walt Disney and Gizmodo calls it fake. No primary source exists; often confused with a real Epcot Horizons line.

answer.label: Not Walt Disney — an unsourced misattribution
answer.authorDates: Walt Disney: 1901–1966 · American animation pioneer & Disney co-founder
answer.sourceLine: Wikiquote files this line in its Misattributed section with no source, and Gizmodo lists it among Disney quotes he never said. The exact wording appears in none of his documented speeches, letters, or films, and no primary source has ever been produced. It is routinely confused online with a different Epcot ‘Horizons’ line, “If you can dream it, you can do it,” which Imagineer Tom Fitzgerald has confirmed he wrote — not Disney.

source.heading: The paper trail

docMeta.dd: Circulates on quote sites, posters & social media; listed as misattributed on Wikiquote

source.excerpt: Laughter is timeless, imagination has no age, and dreams are forever.
trail: Wikiquote’s Walt Disney page places this exact line in its Misattributed section, with no source or citation attached.
Gizmodo’s “8 Walt Disney Quotes That Are Actually Fake” includes this line, noting it is “generically upbeat” and is even sometimes pinned on Tinker Bell instead.

The internet often ‘explains’ the line by citing Imagineer Tom Fitzgerald and the Epcot Horizons ride — but that documentation, per Wikiquote’s citation of Dave Smith’s ‘Ask Dave’, is for a different line, “If you can dream it, you can do it.”
Popular quote aggregators like Goodreads reproduce it as “— Walt Disney” with no source, which is how the misattribution keeps spreading.
source.excerptNote: Widely printed on merchandise and posters under Disney’s name; also sometimes credited to Tinker Bell. No documented instance of Walt Disney writing or speaking it has ever surfaced.
source.rightsNote: The exact wording cannot be tied to any documented Walt Disney work, nor to any other identifiable author, date, or publication. Because its origin is unknown, no copyright status can honestly be asserted — and it is not demonstrably a pre-1931 public-domain text.

author.name: Walt Disney
author.heading: Whose name it carries
author.metaLine: 1901–1966 · American animation pioneer & co-founder of The Walt Disney Company
author.bio: Walter Elias Disney was an American animator, film producer, and entrepreneur who co-founded the Disney studio and pioneered feature animation and the modern theme park. Because his name is shorthand for optimism, wonder, and dreams, feel-good aphorisms are constantly pinned on him — making him one of the internet’s most frequently faked sources. This line is one such case: warmly ‘Disney’ in tone, but absent from his documented words.

misattribution.heading: How the misattribution works
misattribution.intro: This is a textbook ‘magnet-name’ quote: a warm, tidy aphorism about laughter, imagination, and dreams, attached to the one figure who most embodies those words. It reads like Disney — but no documented source has him saying or writing it.

items.why: Printed on merchandise, posters, and shared endlessly on social media as his — yet Wikiquote files it under Misattributed with no source, and Gizmodo lists it among quotes Disney never actually said.
Gizmodo notes the line is sometimes attributed to Tinker Bell — who, in the original Peter Pan film, communicates only in chime sounds and speaks no such words.

items.scope: The confusion with a real Disney-park line
items.why: Some sites ‘source’ this line to Imagineer Tom Fitzgerald and the Horizons ride. But per Dave Smith’s ‘Ask Dave’ (quoted on Wikiquote), Fitzgerald’s confirmed Horizons line is the separate “If you can dream it, you can do it” — not this one, so the citation is a conflation.

misattribution.truthLine: Bottom line: Walt Disney is not a documented source for this wording, and neither is any other identifiable author — per Wikiquote’s Misattributed listing, its true origin is simply unknown.

context.heading: Why it sticks
lead: The line survives because it is perfectly on-brand. Laughter, imagination, and dreams are the exact three notes Disney’s legacy plays, so the sentence feels like a memory of something he must have said — even though the receipts don’t exist.

That plausibility is precisely what makes it durable. Once a warm aphorism and a beloved name fuse on a poster or a meme, each reshare hardens the pairing, and the missing source stops mattering to anyone but the fact-checkers.
context.pull: It sounds like Disney — which is exactly why it isn’t sourced to him.
